Everyone deserves the right to a lawyer to make their best case. Even the justly despised Chicago Parking Meters (CPM) LLC, the singularly uncompromising private consortium of investors currently fleecing Chicagoans after our elected leaders essentially gave away billions of our dollars in what has rightly been called one of the worst acts of municipal governance in the history of municipal governance.

But that to our minds doesn’t excuse the threats this week of leading Chicago attorney Dan Webb against the duly elected representatives of his hometown.

As you likely know, CPM (a group led by Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi) has generated nearly $2 billion in revenue since taking over the city’s roughly 36,000 metered street parking spaces in 2009. It took only 10 years for CPM to recoup its money and yet its lease runs until 2083. As you also likely know, CPM now is trying to sell that super-lucrative lease. Indeed, it has found a private equity buyer in New York-based Stonepeak Partners; the price has yet to be disclosed but is likely somewhere around $3 billion. A nice little exit. We have railed against this deal from hell on half-a-dozen previous occasions.

Alas for CPM, though, there is a clause in the original contract that gives the City Council the right to approve (or not) any buyer in any sale. How much leeway that allows them in practice is a matter of debate; some say very little, others say more than some aldermen (or the Office of the Mayor) might think.

Webb, who represents CPM, is pushing the former view in the interests of his client.

“If the City breaches (the contract),” he wrote in a letter cited in the Tribune and designed to intimidate City Council, “with the result that the sale to Stonepeak collapses, that will destroy value measures in the billions of dollars — for which the City will be held legally responsible.”

We were entertained by the phrase “destroy value,” stated without a possessive.

As if value just floats in thin air and evil aldermen are firing bazookas in its saintly direction. What balderdash.

This is not Chicago’s value. On the contrary, Chicagoans’ parking fees provide that value to, well, Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi, none of whom will be voting in the upcoming aldermanic election.

No value would be destroyed if elements of this contract were revised as part of this sale; it would merely be reapportioned, more fairly in our view.

We’ll add something more that Webb is not bringing up.

If his version of a Chicago fiscal catastrophe came true, then the result would be that Chicago, which already is groaning with liabilities, would find itself pushed to the brink of insolvency, which already is something that was keeping us awake at night even before Grim Reaper Webb started flexing his scythe on behalf of those who have already made billions.

And should Chicago fall into such a state, do you know what would most likely happen to this loathsome parking meter deal?

It would either get a haircut to remember or be rendered null and void.

That would be the one good thing about an insolvent Chicago.

We’re longtime fans of Webb, one of the most distinguished Chicago-trained lawyers. Webb is a former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Illinois and was Special Counsel in the Iran-Contra affair. He has been a force of nature when it comes to fighting corruption. We’ve watched him in the courtroom.

He’s entitled to choose his clients, of course, and this one has big pockets. But not only do we find this a disappointing choice, we wish he were choosing a different tactic.

Lawyers reading our words might say this posturing is all just part of what happens in cases like this. Fair enough. But one party here is the city itself. And we think a lot of Chicagoans would share our discomfort at such words being leveled on the part of a deal that does the city active harm and that hurts the place we all call home.

So, we’ll reiterate what we have said several times. All parties here — the buyer, the seller, the city — should come together and make a reasonable deal for our city; a settlement that involves reasonable concessions (we’ve suggested the rapacious “convenience fee,” often added several times if parking is extended; the lack of flexibility regarding removing parking for community events; and the woefully limited philanthropic footprint of Chicago Parking Meters LLC as good points of reasonable negotiation). Show you care about Chicago, we said to Stonepeak. We’re still waiting for that evidence.

About the only leverage in that contract that remains is the clause relating to its sale. City Council should refuse to be intimidated and not let Webb scare them from using it to help Chicago and its citizens. And we’d prefer to see Webb talk in more reasonable terms of compromise, not with the kind of apocalyptic language that could well come back to hurt his client.
